newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: IVORIAN EXPORTERS SAY COCOA QUALITY KEY TO FUTURE.
newsitem.headline: IVORIAN EXPORTERS SAY COCOA QUALITY KEY TO FUTURE.

text.p: Ivorian exporters want cocoa quality made central to Ivory Coast's licensing of exporters as donor-sponsored marketing reforms gather pace.
"Quality will become an essential element for distinguishing between good and bad exporters," said one pointing to industry concern that market liberalisation meant poor bean quality.
"We are prepared to work on quality," he added, saying an impartial arbiter would be needed to judge performance.

Visiting chocolate industry delegations have said mixing good with poor quality Ivorian cocoa beans to reach an overall export grade of 105 beans per 100 grams with up to eight percent humidity has dented the country's quality image.
Ivory Coast has loosened its monopoly on cocoa and coffee marketing since 1995 under terms for a $150 million agriculture credit from the World Bank -- which wants further changes.
Cocoa and coffee liberalisation are on a wider agenda for donor talks next week on a three-year economic plan for Ivory Coast and its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility.
Donors want the state Caistab commodities board to hand farm-to-port price-setting to the private sector, with exporters possibly assuming a greater role in export auction management.
Ivory Coast has agreed to sweeping coffee marketing reforms from 1998/99, and 1999/2000 for cocoa, but full details have yet to be decided and officially announced.

Ivory Coast licensed around 44 exporters for its 1996/97 marketing season (Oct-Sept) but exporters say only a quarter of them have been regular buyers of export contracts through the state Caistab commodities board auction, set up in May 1996.
"A system of regulation of exporters is needed, dispensing with political considerations," said one exporter.
Donors predict a long-term fall in the number of exporters after some were licensed for 1996/97 despite their unpaid debts to the Caistab and breaches of other export rules.

Government officials say such problems stem partly from closure of upcountry quality checking stations in 1995 and point to the example of Cameroon, where quality dropped off after donor-sponsored reforms there in the early 1990s.
Donors say Ivory Coast has a more developed marketing chain than existed in Cameroon and can weather reforms.
Farmers say quality problems result from a lack of jute sacks, used in storage and transport, since exporters took over control for sack buying and distribution in 1995/96.

Exporters say they are forced to buy sacks from Ivory Coast's only manufacturer, Filtisac, despite a recent relaxation of domestic minimum sack prices by the government. High prices meant they could buy less with their sack allowance of 5 CFA per kilo of coffee or cocoa than if cheaper imports were made available.
"Exporters are not allowed to import. That is the problem," said one exporter. "In principle imports are now allowed (since June) but customs still make them more expensive."

Some exporters had therefore used a black market in Abidjan's Treichville market district, he added, rejecting farmers' crticism that exporters pocketed sack allowances and forced farmers to buy their own.
